1072.title: Like an infant
1072.hook: can you soften your breath like a baby's? give birth without possessing (Tao Te Ching 10)
1072.howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching pair chapter ten with a few minutes of quiet, unforced breathing, letting the breath move on its own instead of controlling it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word and line were the same: stop before it spills, and step back when the work is done.

A baby asleep on a parent's chest. Watch the belly, not the face. It rises, it falls, and nothing else in the body seems to be helping or fighting. No clenched jaw. No shoulders up near the ears. Now check your own breath, right where it is, without fixing it. Is it soft, or is it working? Chapter ten of the Tao Te Ching holds up that sleeping baby as a kind of teacher, and this chapter doesn't instruct. It asks.
screen: `A BABY ASLEEP.` → `WATCH THE BELLY.` → `CHAPTER TEN ASKS.`

segments.voice: First, a string of questions. Can you hold body and spirit together, and not let them drift apart? Can you gather your breath and make it soft, like an infant's? Can you wipe your inner sight clean? Can you care for people without cleverness? The chapter doesn't answer them. They're left open, like a hard question left on the board overnight. Second, why an infant? A baby hasn't learned to brace yet, to hold its breath before a hard conversation or tighten up in traffic. The softness isn't a technique it practiced; it simply hasn't been trained out of it. The chapter seems to ask whether a grown person can find their way back to that, on purpose. Third, softness isn't weakness. Two days ago, chapter eight praised water for doing good without competing. A soft breath has the same quiet strength, small enough to carry in your own chest. Fourth, from breath to what you make. The chapter closes with a list: to give life and not possess it, to act and not lean on it, to lead and not control. The book calls this a hidden kind of virtue. A parent knows its shape: you raise a child, and the child is not yours to own. The soft breath and the open hand sit side by side in the same chapter.
screen: `A CHAPTER OF QUESTIONS.` · `A BABY HASN'T LEARNED TO BRACE.` · `SOFT ISN'T WEAK.` · `GIVE LIFE, AND DON'T POSSESS IT.` · then, large: `CAN YOU MAKE YOUR BREATH SOFT?`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down with one hand on your belly, and let the breath come in without pulling and go out without pushing. Not slow, not deep, only soft, like the sleeping baby's; if you notice bracing in the jaw, the shoulders or the hands, let that one place go. When a thought pulls you away, come back to the hand rising and falling.
Like an infant. Chapter ten's picture for a breath that isn't bracing against anything, and a life that gives without holding on. Today's word.
Your line: soft breath. Nothing to fix, only something to let go of. See you at chapter eleven.

1073.title: Thirty spokes
1073.hook: thirty spokes share a hub, but the empty center makes the wheel useful (Tao Te Ching 11)
1073.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter eleven as a reason to value empty space, in a room, a schedule or a conversation, rather than filling every gap.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was like an infant: a breath that hasn't learned to brace. Your line was soft breath.

An old wooden cart wheel. Spokes run out from the middle like the lines of a sun in a child's drawing, and they all meet in a thick block at the center called the hub. Look closer at the hub. There's a hole through it, where the axle goes. Fill it in with solid wood, make the hub perfect and complete, and the cart goes nowhere. Chapter eleven of the Tao Te Ching starts right there, at the hole in the middle of the wheel.
screen: `AN OLD CART WHEEL.` → `A HOLE IN THE HUB.` → `FILL IT, AND THE CART STOPS.`

segments.voice: First, the wheel. In James Legge's translation, the chapter opens: "The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends." Nave is an old English word for the hub. The spokes are the part you'd photograph. The empty space is the part that turns. Second, two more pictures. A pot is shaped from clay, but you use the hollow inside it. A room is made by cutting doors and windows into walls, and you live in the openings and the space they enclose. Each works because of what isn't there. Third, the two sides together. What is there gives a thing its benefit, the last line says; what isn't there makes it useful. It doesn't say the solid parts don't matter. A wheel with no spokes is just a hole. The wood and the empty space work as a pair. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. A calendar is a kind of wheel. The meetings are the spokes, and they're what people notice. But a day packed solid has no hub left for anything to turn in: no room to think, no gap for someone to call, no pause between one thing and the next. Read this way, the open hour isn't wasted space. It may be the part that lets the rest of the day move.
screen: `THE HOLE IN THE HUB TURNS THE WHEEL.` · `A POT'S HOLLOW, A ROOM'S OPENINGS.` · `WHAT'S THERE, AND WHAT ISN'T, AS A PAIR.` · `AN OPEN HOUR IN A FULL DAY.` · then, large: `THE EMPTY SPACE.`

segments.voice: Look around for an empty space that's doing a job: the inside of a mug, the gap under a door, the floor where people walk. Rest your eyes on it and notice what it makes possible. Then sit in the space this pause makes, with nothing to fill it.
Thirty spokes. Chapter eleven's wheel, where the spokes meet at a hub, and the empty hole in the hub is what lets the wheel turn. Today's word.
Your line: the empty center. The hole in the hub is where the turning happens. Go gently.

1074.title: Five colors
1074.hook: the five colors blind the eye; the sage cares for the belly, not the eye (Tao Te Ching 12)
1074.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twelve as a reason to simplify their surroundings for a while: fewer screens, less noise, plainer food, to let the senses recover.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was thirty spokes: the empty hub is what lets the wheel turn. Your line was the empty center.

A phone screen at the end of a long day. Red badges. A video that starts on its own. A banner sliding down over the banner you were reading. None of it is evil, and some of it is even interesting. And yet, after an hour of it, plain toast can taste like nothing, and a quiet room can feel strangely loud. An old Chinese book, written long before any screen, has a short chapter about exactly this kind of tired: chapter twelve of the Tao Te Ching.
screen: `RED BADGES, AUTOPLAY, BANNERS.` → `TOAST TASTES LIKE NOTHING.` → `CHAPTER TWELVE.`

segments.voice: First, the list. The five colors blind the eye, the chapter says. The five notes deafen the ear. The five flavors dull the mouth. Racing and hunting drive the mind wild. Goods that are hard to get lead people astray. Color, music, food, excitement, treasure: good things, every one. The problem is what too much of them does to the senses that take them in. Second, the strange result. More color, and you see less. More sound, and you hear less. In the chapter's picture, the senses don't get sharper with more input; they go numb, like plain toast after sugar, or a quiet room after a loud one. Third, the turn. So the sage cares for the belly and not the eye. The belly here isn't about overeating; some translators read it as what a person actually needs, set against what only dazzles. The eye wants more to look at. The belly wants enough. Then a short instruction: let go of that, take hold of this. The chapter doesn't spell out which is which; some readers fill it in: that is the dazzle, this is the plain need underneath. Fourth, what it isn't saying. It isn't telling anyone to hate color or give up music. Read this way, it's about the volume knob, not the radio: turn it down, and the senses can come back.
screen: `FIVE COLORS BLIND THE EYE.` · `MORE TO SEE, AND YOU SEE LESS.` · `THE BELLY, NOT THE EYE.` · `THE VOLUME KNOB, NOT THE RADIO.` · then, large: `LET GO OF THAT. TAKE HOLD OF THIS.`

segments.voice: Turn down one thing right now: put the phone face down or in another room, turn off the music or the second screen, or dim a bright light. Then sit with less coming in, and notice what the senses find once they're not flooded: a sound you hadn't heard, a color that was there all along, the taste in your mouth.
Five colors. Chapter twelve's picture of too much: color, sound and flavor that, piled up, leave the senses numb. Today's word.
Your line: less to see. The eye wants more; the belly wants enough. That's chapter twelve.

1075.title: Praise and blame
1075.hook: favor and disgrace both unsettle us; care for the world as for your own body (Tao Te Ching 13)
1075.howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching use chapter thirteen as a check after praise or criticism: they notice how both pull at them, and turn their attention back to the work or the people in front of them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was five colors: too much, and the senses go numb. Your line was less to see.

A cook in a busy kitchen gets two messages from the dining room in the same minute. Table four sends compliments to the chef. Table nine sends a plate back. One feels like sun, the other like a cold draft. An hour later, both are still replaying while the next orders wait, both pulling attention off the stove, both quietly handing the steering wheel to someone in the dining room. Chapter thirteen of the Tao Te Ching puts praise and blame side by side and says something odd: they're the same kind of trouble.
screen: `TWO MESSAGES FROM THE DINING ROOM.` → `COMPLIMENTS, AND A PLATE SENT BACK.` → `THE SAME KIND OF TROUBLE.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. Favor and disgrace both startle a person, the chapter opens. Not just disgrace; favor too. When you get favor, you're startled; when you lose it, you're startled again. Praise isn't a resting place. It's a thing you can now lose. Second, why favor unsettles. The chapter calls favor the lower thing, and readers take this more than one way. Some hear: to be favored is to stand beneath whoever does the favoring, so their approval becomes something you need. Others hear simply that favor is worth less than people think. Either way, praise ties you to someone else's opinion as surely as blame does. Third, the body. Then a startling question: why does a person have great troubles? Because they have a body, a self. If there were no self, what trouble could reach them? Some readers hear this not as a call to give up the body, but as pointing at the part of a person that keeps score of how they're seen, where so much distress gathers. Fourth, the turn outward. Whoever values the whole world the way they value their own body, the chapter ends, can be trusted with the world. The care you'd spend guarding your reputation, spend on everything else instead: from how am I seen, to what needs care.
screen: `FAVOR AND DISGRACE BOTH STARTLE.` · `FAVOR IS THE LOWER THING.` · `TROUBLE GATHERS AROUND THE SELF.` · `CARE FOR THE WORLD AS FOR YOUR BODY.` · then, large: `FAVOR AND DISGRACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a recent compliment and notice where it lands in the body: a warmth, a lift, a small wish to hear it again. Don't push it away or hold on; let it pass like a car on the street outside, and if a criticism shows up instead, treat it the same way. Then let your attention turn to one person or one task that needs care.
Praise and blame. In chapter thirteen, favor and disgrace: two sides of one worry, both of them tied to someone else's opinion. Today's word.
Your line: favor and disgrace. Either one can take the steering wheel, if you let it. That's today, done.

1076.title: Invisible, inaudible
1076.hook: look and it can't be seen, listen and it can't be heard (Tao Te Ching 14)
1076.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching sit with chapter fourteen in silence, listening past the sounds around them to the quiet the sounds come and go in.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was praise and blame: favor and disgrace, both startling. Your line was favor and disgrace.

Three tries. You look for it, and there's nothing to see. You listen for it, and there's nothing to hear. You reach out to grab it, and your hand closes on air. That's how chapter fourteen of the Tao Te Ching begins. It sounds like a riddle, or a ghost story, but it's the book trying, once again, to describe the Tao. Back in chapter one, it said the Tao that can be told isn't the enduring Tao. Today it tries the eyes, the ears and the hands.
screen: `LOOK: NOTHING TO SEE.` → `LISTEN: NOTHING TO HEAR.` → `REACH: AIR.`

segments.voice: First, three names for a failure. What the eye can't find, the chapter calls yi: level and plain, nothing sticking out. What the ear can't catch, it calls xi: faint, rare, almost not there. What the hand can't hold, it calls wei: tiny, subtle. Translators render these in different ways, but each name describes something missing. Second, the three blend into one. They can't be pulled apart and examined; they merge. Not three hidden things, but one thing that escapes every way of grabbing. Third, the shape with no shape. Its top isn't bright, the chapter says, and its bottom isn't dark. Go to meet it and you won't see its front; follow it and you won't see its back. Like looking for the edges of the dark in a room with the lights off: there aren't any to find. Fourth, why bother with something you can't see? Near its end the chapter turns practical: hold on to the ancient way, and you can handle what's in front of you now. Some readers hear this as the point of the riddle: what can't be seen isn't a puzzle to solve but something to rest in. And for the ears there's a small doorway. Silence itself can't be heard, and yet anyone can listen to it.
screen: `YI, XI, WEI: THREE NAMES FOR MISSING.` · `THE THREE BLEND INTO ONE.` · `NO FRONT, NO BACK.` · `HOLD THE OLD WAY, MEET THE NOW.` · then, large: `LOOK, AND IT CAN'T BE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and notice the sounds, a fan, traffic, a voice in another room, your own breath, without naming them for long. Then turn toward the quiet underneath them, the space they appear in and fade back into; you won't hear it, and that's fine. Each time a sound pulls you, let it pass, and listen again for the quiet behind it.
Invisible. In chapter fourteen, what the eye looks for and can't find: the Tao, which escapes seeing, hearing and holding alike. Today's word.
Your line: can't be seen. The quiet behind the sounds was there all along. See you tomorrow.

1077.title: Muddy water
1077.hook: who can make muddy water clear? let it be still (Tao Te Ching 15)
1077.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching use chapter fifteen's image when sitting quietly: instead of trying to clear the mind, they keep still and let the stirred-up thoughts settle on their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was invisible: the Tao escapes seeing, hearing and holding. Your line was can't be seen.

A jar of creek water, shaken up. Brown, cloudy, you can't see your fingers through it. How do you make it clear? Stir it faster? Strain it? Fish out the dirt with a spoon? Each of those keeps the cloud going. The only thing that works feels like doing nothing: set the jar on the counter and leave it alone. Come back later, and the mud lies at the bottom with clear water above it. Chapter fifteen of the Tao Te Ching asks about exactly that jar.
screen: `A SHAKEN JAR OF CREEK WATER.` → `STIR, STRAIN, SPOON?` → `PUT IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, who the chapter describes: the skilled masters of old, so deep they were hard to know. So it describes them from the outside, in pictures: careful, like someone crossing a stream in winter; watchful, like someone wary of the neighbors; reserved, like a guest; loosening, like ice about to melt. And, at the end of the list, murky, like muddy water. Second, the surprise. The masters themselves are compared to muddy water, not crystal, not pure. Some readers hear humility here: the wise don't look wise; they look ordinary, a little unclear, and don't mind. Third, the question, in James Legge's translation: "Who can (make) the muddy water (clear)? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear." The answer isn't a technique. It's stillness and time. You can't hurry a settling; every effort to speed it up stirs the jar again. Fourth, a stirred-up mind. After an argument, bad news, a day of too much, the mind is the shaken jar, and the urge is to fix it right now. Sometimes that's needed. But the chapter points another way: sit, and let the mud find the bottom on its own. Those who hold to this way, it closes, don't want to be full. Room is left for the water to clear.
screen: `THE MASTERS OF OLD, HARD TO KNOW.` · `MURKY, LIKE MUDDY WATER.` · `LET IT BE STILL, AND IT CLEARS.` · `A STIRRED-UP MIND, LEFT ALONE.` · then, large: `LET IT BE STILL.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the body stop moving, and notice whatever is stirred up in you right now: a worry, a plan, the last conversation. Don't strain it or fish anything out; just watch it swirl, the way you'd watch the jar on the counter, for as long as settling takes. You're not making the water clear, only not shaking it.
Muddy water. Chapter fifteen's jar: you can't stir it clear, but let it be still, and it clears on its own. Today's word.
Your line: let it settle. Stillness and time do what stirring can't. Back tomorrow, same hill.

pairs: like crossing a stream in winter

1078.title: Return to the root
1078.hook: reach utmost emptiness, hold to stillness; all things return to their root (Tao Te Ching 16)
1078.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter sixteen as a guide to sitting still: they watch thoughts and sensations rise and fall away, and keep coming back to the quiet beneath them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was muddy water: you can't stir it clear, but left still, it clears. Your line was let it settle.

Down, in, quieter, emptier. Lay this week's chapters side by side and that's the direction they keep pointing: a cup not filled to the brim, a soft breath like a sleeping baby's, the hole in a wheel's hub, too many colors and a numb eye, praise and blame both startling, something you look for and can't see, a jar of muddy water set down to clear. Chapter sixteen of the Tao Te Ching, today's chapter, names where that direction leads. It calls it the root.
screen: `SOFT BREATH. THE EMPTY CENTER. LESS TO SEE.` → `FAVOR AND DISGRACE. CAN'T BE SEEN. LET IT SETTLE.` → `DOWN, IN, QUIETER.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. The chapter opens by asking for emptiness taken as far as it goes, and stillness held steadily. Not a picture this time, but something close to a method: empty out, and keep still. Second, what you see from there. From that stillness, you watch all things rise and watch them return. Things grow and flourish, and each goes back to its root. A leaf comes out in spring and falls in autumn. A thought appears and fades. A wave lifts and sinks back into the sea. The rising is real. So is the going back. Third, the chain. Then a short ladder. Returning to the root is stillness. Stillness is going back to what you're meant to be. That is the constant. Knowing the constant is called clear seeing. Not knowing it, the chapter warns, people act blindly and bring trouble on themselves. Each step leans on the one before, so it's worth reading slowly. Fourth, comfort as well as teaching. Whoever knows the constant, the chapter ends, becomes open, and from openness comes fairness, and so on, step by step, up to the Tao, which lasts. To the end of one's life, it says, there is no danger. Some readers hear reassurance as much as instruction. Things go back where they came from. You don't have to drag yourself there. You return.
screen: `EMPTINESS AS FAR AS IT GOES.` · `ALL THINGS RISE, AND RETURN.` · `THE ROOT IS STILLNESS.` · `KNOWING THE CONSTANT IS CLEAR SEEING.` · then, large: `EACH RETURNS TO ITS ROOT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath be soft, the way it was on the first day of this week, and watch what rises: a sound, a thought, an itch, a memory. Don't follow it out; watch it come up and sink back, the way a wave returns to the sea. Each time you notice you've wandered, that noticing is the return, so come back to the stillness and rest there.
Return to the root. Chapter sixteen's picture: everything that rises goes back where it came from, and that going back is stillness. Today's word.
Your line: return to the root. Whatever rises goes back where it came from. Until tomorrow.
